questions.q: Why can a host that scores 98% on a CIS Benchmark scan still run a dangerously insecure container?
options: CIS Benchmark scores are always inaccurate and cannot be trusted for any system
A 98% score means the host is only 2% functional
A container is a process created from an image that may have no hardening applied at all, and host-level benchmarks were never designed to check what's inside or how it's configured
Containers are immune to all security vulnerabilities by design
questions.explain: Host hardening (CIS Benchmark, sysctl settings, Ansible roles) governs the host. None of it reaches inside a container's image or runtime configuration.

questions.q: Why does running a container's main process as root inside the container matter for security, even though the container is isolated from the host?
options: Running as root inside a container has no security implications whatsoever
If an attacker escapes the container's isolation through a kernel vulnerability or misconfigured mount, running as root inside gives them a running start on becoming root outside too
It is impossible to run a container process as anything other than root
Containers running as root automatically get slower performance, which is the only downside
questions.explain: A USER directive or --user flag sets an explicit non-root UID, reducing what an attacker gains if they manage to break out of the container.

questions.q: What does a read-only root filesystem protect against, and how is it set?
options: It is the default behavior for every container with no configuration needed
It only applies to the host's filesystem, never the container's
It blocks a compromised process from writing a backdoor or modifying application code in place, set with docker run --read-only or securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem in Kubernetes
It prevents the container from ever starting up successfully
questions.explain: A read-only root filesystem seals the container's filesystem against in-place tampering; any legitimate writes go to an explicitly mounted volume instead.

questions.q: What does the CIS Docker Benchmark recommend regarding Linux capabilities in a container?
options: Capabilities cannot be modified for containers under any circumstances
Capabilities only apply to virtual machines, not containers
Grant every available capability by default to avoid breaking functionality
Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones actually needed, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
questions.explain: Linux capabilities split root's all-or-nothing privilege into separate grants; best practice is --cap-drop=ALL plus explicitly adding back only what's required.

questions.q: What problem does image scanning with a tool like Trivy address that non-root, read-only, and dropped-capability settings do not?
options: It replaces the need for any runtime hardening settings entirely
It automatically fixes every vulnerability in an image without any further action
It checks what's actually installed inside the image against known CVE databases, catching vulnerabilities independent of how carefully the container is run at runtime
It only works on images that are already known to be completely secure
questions.explain: Non-root, read-only, and capability settings describe how a container runs. Image scanning addresses what's inside the image itself, such as outdated OS packages carrying known CVEs.
